topic.title: Education: Measurement and evidence in Community Learning Centres

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The five Community Learning Centres in Leicester are run by a charity called Learn Leicester. For many years the staff kept very few records. They believed that the classes helped people, but they could not show it. In 2021 the city council asked a hard question. It wanted to know what really changed for students after their courses. The charity could not answer with numbers. So it gave one member of staff, Amina Hassan, a new job: to collect evidence.

sections.heading: How it operates
sections.text: Amina started a simple system in January 2022. Every student signs in on a card at the door, so the centres know who comes and how often. On the first day of a course, students take a short test and answer six questions about their confidence. They take the same test again on the last day. Six months later, Amina telephones about one student in five. The call takes ten minutes. She asks three things: do they have a job, are they still studying, and do they use their new skills at home?

sections.heading: Evidence and experience
sections.text: The first full report came out in March 2024. It covered 1,860 students. Reading scores went up for 71% of the students in the English classes. In the computer courses, the number of people who could send an email alone rose from 24% to 89%. Nine months after finishing, 340 students had found paid work. Yusuf Ali, a taxi driver, took the accounts course in 2023. He now does the accounts for his small taxi business himself. Students also came more often than the staff expected: the average student attended 22 of the 24 lessons.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: Measuring is harder than it looks. Many students leave before the last lesson, so there is no second test for them. About one third of the phone numbers no longer work after six months. Some students do not want to answer questions about money or work. Confidence is difficult to measure at all, because people judge themselves in different ways. The work also costs money. The report cost £14,000, which is the price of two part-time teachers for a year, and some staff think that this money should go to classes instead.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text: The charity is now making its system simpler. From September, students will answer four questions instead of six, on a tablet at the door. Two researchers from De Montfort University will check the results every year, so the numbers do not come only from the charity itself. Amina also wants to follow one group of 200 students for three years, not six months. The next report will appear on the charity's website in 2027. “If we cannot measure our work, we cannot improve it,” Amina says.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — Background
The five Community Learning Centres in Leicester are run by a charity called Learn Leicester. For many years the staff kept very few records. They believed that the classes helped people, but they could not show it. In 2021 the city council asked a hard question. It wanted to know what really changed for students after their courses. The charity could not answer with numbers. So it gave one member of staff, Amina Hassan, a new job: to collect evidence.

Paragraph 2 — How it operates
Amina started a simple system in January 2022. Every student signs in on a card at the door, so the centres know who comes and how often. On the first day of a course, students take a short test and answer six questions about their confidence. They take the same test again on the last day. Six months later, Amina telephones about one student in five. The call takes ten minutes. She asks three things: do they have a job, are they still studying, and do they use their new skills at home?

Paragraph 3 — Evidence and experience
The first full report came out in March 2024. It covered 1,860 students. Reading scores went up for 71% of the students in the English classes. In the computer courses, the number of people who could send an email alone rose from 24% to 89%. Nine months after finishing, 340 students had found paid work. Yusuf Ali, a taxi driver, took the accounts course in 2023. He now does the accounts for his small taxi business himself. Students also came more often than the staff expected: the average student attended 22 of the 24 lessons.

Paragraph 4 — Challenges
Measuring is harder than it looks. Many students leave before the last lesson, so there is no second test for them. About one third of the phone numbers no longer work after six months. Some students do not want to answer questions about money or work. Confidence is difficult to measure at all, because people judge themselves in different ways. The work also costs money. The report cost £14,000, which is the price of two part-time teachers for a year, and some staff think that this money should go to classes instead.

Paragraph 5 — Next steps
The charity is now making its system simpler. From September, students will answer four questions instead of six, on a tablet at the door. Two researchers from De Montfort University will check the results every year, so the numbers do not come only from the charity itself. Amina also wants to follow one group of 200 students for three years, not six months. The next report will appear on the charity's website in 2027. “If we cannot measure our work, we cannot improve it,” Amina says.
